📊 Visa finds 46% in Asia Pacific may use stablecoins by 2031 

📣 Stablecoin interest has moved well ahead of actual use across Asia Pacific, with 46% of surveyed consumers saying they are likely to use the tokens within five years compared with 16% who used them during the past year. The research found strong interest in using stablecoins for online purchases, travel, overseas shopping and moving money across borders. Yet the survey showed a large knowledge gap, with only 6% of respondents demonstrating what Visa described as an accurate understanding of how stablecoins work.

⭐️ Across the 14 markets, 46% of respondents said they were likely to use stablecoins during the next five years. Only 16% reported using them during the previous 12 months. Visa did not disclose in its release what those existing users had used stablecoins for. The 16% figure could therefore include trading, transfers, payments or other cryptocurrency activity and should not be treated solely as consumer payment adoption.

‼️ Cross-border transfers produced one of the strongest future-use readings. Around 49% of respondents said they thought stablecoins could become a common method of moving money between countries within five years. Visa Head of Digital Currencies for Asia Pacific Nischint Sanghavi said consumers were starting to consider stablecoins for “online purchases, travel and cross-border transfers.” The company views those uses as potential extensions of existing payment behavior.

Crypto Idea

AI could crack Bitcoin in just a few months

That’s the claim making the rounds right now following a statement by an Ethereum Foundation researcher. It sounds scary, but there’s still a huge gap between this kind of threat and an actual hack.

For that to happen, AI would need to learn how to derive a private key from publicly available wallet information and gain access to someone else’s coins. No one has demonstrated a way to do that yet. AI can already solve some incredibly difficult mathematical problems, but solving a problem that humans couldn’t crack before is one thing, and discovering a new mathematical method that breaks the foundation of modern data security is something entirely different.

And this is where the main point often gets lost. If such a method actually emerges, Bitcoin won’t be the only thing at risk. The security of banking apps, payment systems, websites, mobile networks, messaging apps, and a huge part of our digital infrastructure would all be called into question. In other words, it wouldn’t just be a crypto crisis, but a crisis for the entire modern digital security system.

At the same time, even within Bitcoin, things aren’t so straightforward. Different types of wallets work differently, and some are better protected against this kind of scenario. Bitcoin itself could also be upgraded to adopt new security methods if the threat becomes real. That’s exactly why developers discuss these scenarios in advance, rather than waiting until something actually happens.

So the claim that AI will simply crack Bitcoin in a few months looks more like a bet on an extraordinarily rapid technological breakthrough than a realistic forecast. It makes sense to prepare for such a scenario. But it’s definitely too early to conclude that Bitcoin is about to stop working.

And the situation can be viewed from a completely different angle. Today, crypto doesn’t just carry technological risks; it also protects against a wide range of risks associated with the traditional system. Banking, political, geopolitical, and currency risks. It allows people to store and move capital without being entirely dependent on a particular bank or government.

That’s why yet another Bitcoin scare story doesn’t change the bigger picture. No asset is risk-free. The question is always which specific risks each instrument helps protect against. And in a world where problems with banks, governments, and currencies keep piling up, the role of an asset independent of them looks more important than ever.

The “Bread and Butter” Parable

A husband and wife had been married for thirty years. Every year on their anniversary, she baked a small loaf of bread, just as she had done that morning.

At breakfast, she cut the loaf in half, buttered both pieces, and—as always—was about to give her husband the crusty end. But halfway through, she stopped. “On our thirtieth anniversary, I want the crust for myself,” she thought. “I’ve dreamed of it for thirty years, and I’ve earned it. I’ve been a devoted wife, raised wonderful sons, and kept our home in order.”

So she gave him the soft middle instead—a first in all their years together. He took it and smiled. “What a wonderful gift you’ve given me today! I’ve loved the soft middle since I was a child, but you always took it, so I never dared say anything.”

Moral: True love is found where both people know how to give more than they take.

Tomorrow’s forecast: motivation is expected, though delays are possible.

Tomorrow is Monday, which means millions of people will once again try to start the workweek with a “fresh start.” On Sunday evening, it all seems perfectly doable: clear the backlog, sort through your inbox, kick off an important project—and maybe even be a little more successful by Wednesday.

But things can look different by morning. At 9:00, colleagues start calling. By 9:30, you’ve uncovered a few urgent issues no one had even mentioned on Friday. By 11:00, you’ve sat through ten calls and a meeting that produced yet more tasks. And as lunchtime approaches, you realize you haven’t even started on your own plans. Somehow, you’re already tired, even though you’ve barely made a dent in what you set out to do.

In other words, a perfectly ordinary Monday. It’s a tough day, but what’s almost funny is how many of us expect to begin the week with a surge of motivation. We’ll wake up, have a coffee, feel ready to work—and then get started.

But motivation has one inconvenient habit: it doesn’t have to show up before you take action. Often, it works the other way around. You start on a task, make some progress, get a clearer sense of what comes next—and gradually, the urge to keep going follows.

So let’s be practical. Tomorrow, don’t waste time looking for inspiration in interviews with successful entrepreneurs or spending the first hour crafting the perfect plan. Just choose one genuinely important task tonight and decide on the first concrete step. Not “work on the project,” but something like drafting the first three pages of a proposal, checking the figures, or sending that email you’ve been putting off.

Tomorrow, try to give that task at least the first 25–30 minutes of your day, before diving into other people’s requests, messages, and endless discussions—if your job allows it, of course. You don’t have to fix everything that piled up last week in a single morning. By lunchtime, one tangible result is far more valuable than ten beautifully worded intentions.

One more thing: don’t measure your productivity by how many hours you’ve been busy. You can spend all day replying to messages, attending meetings, and feeling indispensable without getting any closer to your own goals.

So if motivation is late for work again tomorrow, try starting without it. Maybe it’s just used to showing up after everything’s already done.
